On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command

- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings

> **Explanation:**
> - **Option C** is correct. By inserting the new binding `a ↦ τ₂` at the **head** of the collision chain, it shadows the older binding `a ↦ τ₁`. Lookups will f
ind the new binding first (which is the correct semantics — inner scopes shadow outer scopes).
> - This is also the most efficient approach — O(1) insertion at the head.
> - Option A requires traversing the entire chain to find and overwrite, which is slower.
> - Option B puts the new binding at the end, which means lookups must traverse past old bindings first — semantically wrong and inefficient.

> **Answer: symbol**
>
> **Explanation:**
> - The Tiger compiler uses the **Symbol** module to convert string identifiers into **symbols** (unique pointer-based identifiers).
> - This provides three key optimizations:
>   1. **Hash key extraction** is very fast — the symbol pointer itself serves as the integer hash key.
>   2. **Equality comparison** is fast — just compare pointers/integers instead of character-by-character string comparison.
>   3. **Ordering comparison** is fast — needed for binary search trees.
> - The presentation interface defines: `S_symbol S_symbol(string)`, `string S_name(S_symbol)`, with symbol interning to ensure each unique string has exactly o
ne symbol.

> - B) Each class has its own symbol table, combined into comprehensive environment σ₇
> - C) Strict sequential processing order
> - D) Stack-based symbol table
>
> **Answer: B**
>
> **Explanation:**
> - **Option B** is correct. Each class (E, N, D) has its own symbol table (σ₁, σ₃, σ₅). These are combined into a comprehensive environment `σ₇ = σ₂ + σ₄ + σ₆`
 that represents the entire package.
> - All classes are compiled within this combined environment `σ₇`, which means all symbols are visible to each other, allowing forward references.
> - Option A is incorrect because Java maintains per-class symbol tables for encapsulation; a single global table would break scoping rules.
> - Option C is incorrect because Java allows forward references — classes don't need to be processed in strict source order.
> - Option D is incorrect because the stack-based approach doesn't handle cross-class references.
>
> ---
>
> ## 5. Summary
>
> | Concept | Functional Style | Imperative Style |
> |---|---|---|
> | **Insertion** | Creates new structure, preserves old | Mutates in place |
> | **Restore** | Point to old structure | Undo stack / prevtop chain |
> | **Data Structure** | Balanced BST | Hash table with chaining |
> | **Overhead** | Copy nodes along insertion path | Pointer manipulation |
> | **Tiger Compiler** | Not used | Used (with hash tables) |
>
> The Tiger compiler implements **imperative-style** symbol tables with:
> 1. **Hash tables** for O(1) average-case lookups
> 2. **Symbol interning** for fast string-to-symbol conversion
> 3. **Auxiliary stack or prevtop integration** for scope management
> 4. **External chaining** for hash collision resolution, with new bindings inserted at the head to shadow older ones
